newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels turn screws on Mobutu, issue ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Rebels turn screws on Mobutu, issue ultimatum.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels tightened the screws on Zaire's veteran strongman Mobutu Sese Seko, consolidating their hold on its economic heart and giving him three days to start talks on quitting.
Rebels forces ended the battle for the nation's southern second city Lubumbashi on Thursday, driving Mobutu loyalists from its airport and sending them fleeing into the bush.

In Kinshasa Mobutu, who has held sway over Africa's third largest country since seizing power 1965, had talks with his new military prime minister General Likulia Bolongo. The city was calm one day after his army clashed with opposition loyalists.
But former colonial power Belgium accused Mobutu of engineering a military coup to cling on to power and denounced what it called "a military dictatorship".
France, a long-time Mobutu ally, called for an orderly transition and questioned Kabila's democratic credentials -- casting doubts on whether he would call elections.

"I am waiting for a little period of three days for Mobutu to make a decision to contact us to negotiate his departure," Kabila told a news conference at Mobutu's former palace in the eastern town Goma, now used as rebel headquarters.

Kabila said he awaited "good news on the willingness of Mobutu to depart", adding that Mobutu knew how to get in touch. "If this doesn't happen we will be forced to advance on all fronts," Kabila said.

The rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, now control about half of Zaire -- including the key diamond province of Kasai and most of the southern copper and cobalt mining province of Shaba.

Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August, declared a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday and appointed Likulia on Wednesday, but he has not been seen in public for several days.
State television said he and Likulia discussed the new prime minister's proposed government.

The United States, which helped prop up Mobutu during the Cold War fearing the spread of communism in strategic parts of Africa, says it was time for the veteran strongman to go. The State Department has urged an end to "dictatorship" in Zaire.

Belgium condemned Mobutu's appointment of a general to be prime minister as "military dictatorship revisited". Its Foreign Minister Erik Derycke said in Brussels Mobutu was clinging on desperately to power.
"It seems that President Mobutu, with his coup d'etat, has returned to the point he started out at more than 30 years ago."
France called for an orderly transition towards elections, but Prime Minister Alain Juppe questioned Kabila's democratic credentials in a magazine interview.
"When you hear (Kabila) say there won't be an election, that the people must first 'become sensitive to the doctrine', you can only worry about what it means," he told Figaro-Magazine.
In Lubumbashi, rebels consolidated their grip on the city one day after moving into it.
They flushed Mobutu loyalists out of the airport after a 90-minute gunfight and cracked down on lawlessness. Doctors said seven youths had been shot dead while defying a ban on looting.
A disciplined column of boy soldiers marched into the city like battle-hardened soldiers but their youth shone through when well-wishers offered ice lollipops -- which they demolished thirstily.
